sections.readable_text:
How many fluid ounces are equivalent to [MATH: 25\,\textrm{qt}?]

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{cup} = 8\,\textrm{fl oz}] and [MATH: 1\,\textrm{qt} = 4 \, \textrm{cups}]

sections.normalized_html:
We want to convert the volume from quarts to fluid ounces.

We are also given that there are [MATH: 8] fluid ounces per cup, which we can write as follows: [MATH: \dfrac{8 \, \textrm{fl oz}}{\textrm{cup}}]

In the same way, we are given that there are [MATH: 4] cups per quart, which we can write as follows: [MATH: \dfrac{4 \, \textrm{cups}}{\textrm{qt}}]

To convert quarts to fluid ounces, we multiply the given value by the conversion factors above. So, multiplying [MATH: 25\,\textrm{qt}] by our conversion factors, we get [MATH: 25qt|= 25qt ⋅ (8fl oz)/(cup) ⋅ (4cups)/(qt); = 25qt ⋅ (8fl oz)/(cup) ⋅ (4cups)/(qt); = 25 ⋅ 8 ⋅ 4fl oz; = 800fl oz.]

Therefore, [MATH: 25\,\textrm{qt}] is equivalent to [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{800}\,\textrm{fl oz}.]

sections.normalized_html:
A race is [MATH: 44] furlongs [MATH: (\textrm{fur})] long. How many feet is this distance?

sections.readable_text:
A race is [MATH: 44] furlongs [MATH: (\textrm{fur})] long. How many feet is this distance?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{fur} = 220\,\textrm{yd}] and [MATH: 1\,\textrm{yd} = 3\,\textrm{ft}]

sections.normalized_html:
We are given the units [MATH: \textrm{fur},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \textrm{ft}.] We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

[MATH: \textrm{fur}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{ft}]

One of the conversion factors should change [MATH: \textrm{fur}] to [MATH: \textrm{yd}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{fur}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\cancel{\textrm{fur}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{ft}]

The other conversion factor should change [MATH: \textrm{yd}] into [MATH: \textrm{ft}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{fur}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{yd}}}{\cancel{\textrm{fur}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{ft} }{ \cancel{\textrm{yd}} } = \textrm{ft}]

So, our conversion formula is [MATH: \textrm{fur} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\textrm{fur} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{ft} }{ \textrm{yd} } = \textrm{ft}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

  • The length given in the problem statement is [MATH: 44 \, \textrm{fur}.]

  • We are given that there are [MATH: 220] yards per furlong.

  • We are also given that there are [MATH: 3] feet per yard.

Applying our conversion formula, we have [MATH: 44fur|= 44fur ⋅ 220(yd)/(fur) ⋅ 3(ft)/(yd); = (44 ⋅ 220 ⋅ 3)fur ⋅ (yd)/(fur) ⋅ (ft)/(yd); = 29, 040ft.]

Therefore, [MATH: 44\,\textrm{fur}] is equivalent to [MATH: 29,040\,\textrm{ft}.]

sections.normalized_html:
A group of friends is hiking a trail. Its steepest section is [MATH: 880\,\textrm{ft}] long. How long is this section in miles?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{yd} = 3\,\textrm{ft}] and [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}]
sections.readable_text:

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{yd} = 3\,\textrm{ft}] and [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}]

sections.normalized_html:
We are given the units [MATH: \textrm{ft},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \textrm{mi}.] We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

[MATH: \textrm{ft}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{mi}]

One of the conversion factors should change [MATH: \textrm{ft}] to [MATH: \textrm{yd}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{ft}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\cancel{\textrm{ft}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{mi}]

The other conversion factor should change [MATH: \textrm{yd}] into [MATH: \textrm{mi}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{ft}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{yd}}}{\cancel{\textrm{ft}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{mi} }{ \cancel{\textrm{yd}} } = \textrm{mi}]

So, our conversion formula is [MATH: \textrm{ft} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\textrm{ft} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{mi} }{ \textrm{yd} } = \textrm{mi}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

  • The length given in the problem statement is [MATH: 880 \, \textrm{ft}.]

  • We are given that there are [MATH: 3] feet per yard. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{3}] yards per foot.

  • We are also given that there are [MATH: 1,760] yards per mile. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1,760}] miles per yard.

Applying our conversion formula, we have [MATH: 880ft|= 880ft ⋅ (1)/(3)(yd)/(ft) ⋅ (1)/(1, 760)(mi)/(yd); = (880 ⋅ (1)/(3) ⋅ (1)/(1, 760))ft ⋅ (yd)/(ft) ⋅ (mi)/(yd); = ((880)/(3) ⋅ (1)/(1, 760))mi; = (1)/(6)mi.]

Therefore, the steepest section is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}\,\textrm{mi}] long.

items.title: Converting Between Currencies and Finding a Markdown

sections.normalized_html: Mateo has [MATH: 310] British pounds [MATH: (\textrm{£}310)] that he wants to exchange for US dollars at a currency kiosk. The exchange rate is [MATH: \textrm{£}1 = \[math]1.34.] The kiosk charges a [MATH: 2.5\%] fee on the converted US dollar amount. How many US dollars will Mateo receive after the [MATH: 2.5\%] fee?
sections.readable_text: Mateo has [MATH: 310] British pounds [MATH: (\textrm{£}310)] that he wants to exchange for US dollars at a currency kiosk. The exchange rate is [MATH: \textrm{£}1 = \[math]1.34.] The kiosk charges a [MATH: 2.5\%] fee on the converted US dollar amount. How many US dollars will Mateo receive after the [MATH: 2.5\%] fee?

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that [MATH: \textrm{£}1] is equivalent to [MATH: \[math]1.34.] So, to convert [MATH: \textrm{£}310] to US dollars, we multiply it by the exchange rate: [MATH: 310 \cdot 1.34 = 415.4] Therefore, [MATH: \textrm{£}310] is equivalent to [MATH: \[/math]415.4.]

Now, because Mateo pays a [MATH: 2.5\%] fee on the converted amount, he receives [MATH: (100 - 2.5)\% = 97.5\%] of the converted US dollars.

Finally, since [MATH: 415.4 \cdot 97.5\% = 415.4 \cdot 0.975 = 405.015,] we conclude that Mateo receives a total of [MATH: \[math]405.015] after the conversion.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we’ll practice multi-step unit conversions.

---

Item 2 — Example: Converting Units of Volume to Smaller Units

Example Prompt:
How many fluid ounces are equivalent to [MATH: 25\,\textrm{qt}?]

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{cup} = 8\,\textrm{fl oz}] and [MATH: 1\,\textrm{qt} = 4 \, \textrm{cups}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We want to convert the volume from quarts to fluid ounces.

We are also given that there are [MATH: 8] fluid ounces per cup, which we can write as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{8 \, \textrm{fl oz}}{\textrm{cup}}]

In the same way, we are given that there are [MATH: 4] cups per quart, which we can write as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{4 \, \textrm{cups}}{\textrm{qt}}]

To convert quarts to fluid ounces, we multiply the given value by the conversion factors above. So, multiplying [MATH: 25\,\textrm{qt}] by our conversion factors, we get
[MATH: 25qt|= 25qt ⋅ (8fl oz)/(cup) ⋅ (4cups)/(qt); = 25qt ⋅ (8fl oz)/(cup) ⋅ (4cups)/(qt); = 25 ⋅ 8 ⋅ 4fl oz; = 800fl oz.]

Therefore, [MATH: 25\,\textrm{qt}] is equivalent to [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{800}\,\textrm{fl oz}.]

Item 5 — Example: Converting Units of Length to Smaller Units

Example Prompt:
A race is [MATH: 44] furlongs [MATH: (\textrm{fur})] long. How many feet is this distance?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{fur} = 220\,\textrm{yd}] and [MATH: 1\,\textrm{yd} = 3\,\textrm{ft}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given the units [MATH: \textrm{fur},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \textrm{ft}.] We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

[MATH: \textrm{fur}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{ft}]

One of the conversion factors should change [MATH: \textrm{fur}] to [MATH: \textrm{yd}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{fur}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\cancel{\textrm{fur}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{ft}]

The other conversion factor should change [MATH: \textrm{yd}] into [MATH: \textrm{ft}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{fur}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{yd}}}{\cancel{\textrm{fur}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{ft} }{ \cancel{\textrm{yd}} } = \textrm{ft}]

So, our conversion formula is
[MATH: \textrm{fur} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\textrm{fur} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{ft} }{ \textrm{yd} } = \textrm{ft}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

- The length given in the problem statement is [MATH: 44 \, \textrm{fur}.]
- We are given that there are [MATH: 220] yards per furlong.
- We are also given that there are [MATH: 3] feet per yard.

Applying our conversion formula, we have
[MATH: 44fur|= 44fur ⋅ 220(yd)/(fur) ⋅ 3(ft)/(yd); = (44 ⋅ 220 ⋅ 3)fur ⋅ (yd)/(fur) ⋅ (ft)/(yd); = 29, 040ft.]

Therefore, [MATH: 44\,\textrm{fur}] is equivalent to [MATH: 29,040\,\textrm{ft}.]

Item 8 — Example: Converting Units of Length to Larger Units

Example Prompt:
A group of friends is hiking a trail. Its steepest section is [MATH: 880\,\textrm{ft}] long. How long is this section in miles?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{yd} = 3\,\textrm{ft}] and [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given the units [MATH: \textrm{ft},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \textrm{mi}.] We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

[MATH: \textrm{ft}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{mi}]

One of the conversion factors should change [MATH: \textrm{ft}] to [MATH: \textrm{yd}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{ft}} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\cancel{\textrm{ft}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \textrm{mi}]

The other conversion factor should change [MATH: \textrm{yd}] into [MATH: \textrm{mi}.]

[MATH: \cancel{\textrm{ft}} \cdot \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{yd}}}{\cancel{\textrm{ft}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{mi} }{ \cancel{\textrm{yd}} } = \textrm{mi}]

So, our conversion formula is
[MATH: \textrm{ft} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{yd}}{\textrm{ft} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{mi} }{ \textrm{yd} } = \textrm{mi}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

- The length given in the problem statement is [MATH: 880 \, \textrm{ft}.]
- We are given that there are [MATH: 3] feet per yard. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{3}] yards per foot.
- We are also given that there are [MATH: 1,760] yards per mile. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1,760}] miles per yard.

Applying our conversion formula, we have
[MATH: 880ft|= 880ft ⋅ (1)/(3)(yd)/(ft) ⋅ (1)/(1, 760)(mi)/(yd); = (880 ⋅ (1)/(3) ⋅ (1)/(1, 760))ft ⋅ (yd)/(ft) ⋅ (mi)/(yd); = ((880)/(3) ⋅ (1)/(1, 760))mi; = (1)/(6)mi.]

Therefore, the steepest section is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}\,\textrm{mi}] long.

Item 11 — Example: Converting Between Currencies and Finding a Markdown

Example Prompt:
Mateo has [MATH: 310] British pounds [MATH: (\textrm{£}310)] that he wants to exchange for US dollars at a currency kiosk. The exchange rate is [MATH: \textrm{£}1 = \[math]1.34.] The kiosk charges a [MATH: 2.5\%] fee on the converted US dollar amount. How many US dollars will Mateo receive after the [MATH: 2.5\%] fee?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are told that [MATH: \textrm{£}1] is equivalent to [MATH: \[math]1.34.] So, to convert [MATH: \textrm{£}310] to US dollars, we multiply it by the exchange rate:
[MATH: 310 \cdot 1.34 = 415.4]
Therefore, [MATH: \textrm{£}310] is equivalent to [MATH: \[/math]415.4.]

Now, because Mateo pays a [MATH: 2.5\%] fee on the converted amount, he receives
[MATH: (100 - 2.5)\% = 97.5\%]
of the converted US dollars.

Finally, since
[MATH: 415.4 \cdot 97.5\% = 415.4 \cdot 0.975 = 405.015,]
we conclude that Mateo receives a total of [MATH: \[math]405.015] after the conversion.
